questions.stem: Who is the subject of the documentary Gurrumul?
options: A Darwin record producer who built a label for Indigenous musicians from remote communities
A Western Desert actor who starred in a series of famous Australian films
A Yolngu singer from Elcho Island, blind from birth, who became famous worldwide
A Torres Strait Islander painter who became famous worldwide for his huge public murals
questions.explanation: Geoffrey Gurrumul Yunupingu was a Yolngu man from Galiwin'ku on Elcho Island, in north-east Arnhem Land. Blind from birth, he became one of Australia's most celebrated singers.

questions.stem: Which best describes the shape of the documentary?
options: It is built around his final illness, tracing his health from diagnosis to his death
It is a series of interviews with famous musicians who worked with him over the years
It follows his life from childhood on Elcho Island to his solo fame and last project
It covers one single concert tour of Europe, filmed over a few weeks in one year
questions.explanation: The film moves from his early life and his time in Yothu Yindi and the Saltwater Band to his solo career after his 2008 album, and ends with his final orchestral project.

questions.stem: What is notable about when the film was finished?
options: It was finished in time for him to attend its premiere in Berlin
Gurrumul approved the final cut days before he died in 2017
It was finished ten years after his death by a new director
It was finished after his death, without his approval of the final cut
questions.explanation: The director has said the film was finished three days before Gurrumul died. Only the opening title cards and an end graphic were changed afterwards.

questions.stem: On the eve of his first planned tour of the United States, what does Gurrumul do?
options: He agrees to go on condition that his whole family can travel with him on the tour
He doesn't turn up at Darwin airport, staying on Elcho Island for family business
He cancels the tour to record a new album with a famous American producer
He flies to the United States alone, without telling Hohnen or the band
questions.explanation: Gurrumul stays home for family reasons, and Michael Hohnen is left phoning the American promoters. Even Hohnen admits he can never book a major international tour again.

questions.stem: On a French television show, Gurrumul sings 'Every Breath You Take' in his own language with Sting. What does the scene reveal?
options: The French audience's confusion at hearing a famous English song sung in a Yolngu language
The gap between celebrity culture and what mattered to Gurrumul, who didn't know who Sting was
Gurrumul's admiration for Sting, whose songs had inspired him to perform as a young man
The pressure Sting put on Gurrumul to sing in English rather than in his own language
questions.explanation: Gurrumul performs with one of the world's most famous singers without knowing who he is. The scene is awkward to watch, and it shows how little the industry's idea of fame meant to him.

questions.stem: What is the final musical project the film shows?
options: A live album recorded on a farewell tour with the Saltwater Band
Traditional Yolngu songs arranged for orchestra with composer Erkki Veltheim
A country music album recorded in Nashville with American session musicians and singers
A tour of Yothu Yindi's hit songs played with the band's original members
questions.explanation: Gurrumul worked with Erkki Veltheim to set Yolngu songs for orchestra. The result, Djarimirri, came out after his death and is the emotional peak of the film.

questions.stem: The album that came from his last project, Djarimirri, made history after his death. How?
options: It was the first album he recorded without Michael Hohnen as his producer
It was the first of his albums to include songs sung in English as well as Yolngu
It was the first album in an Australian Indigenous language to reach number one in Australia
It was the first Australian album to win a Grammy Award for the best orchestral recording
questions.explanation: Djarimirri reached number one on the ARIA albums chart in 2018, the first album in an Australian Indigenous language to do so. The film builds to this music.

questions.stem: Who is Michael Hohnen?
options: Gurrumul's uncle, a senior Yolngu elder who taught him the traditional songs of his clan
A journalist who travelled with Gurrumul to write a book about his life
The film's director, who also narrates the story in voiceover
Gurrumul's friend, producer and fellow musician, who often speaks for him
questions.explanation: Hohnen, a double bass player, worked with Gurrumul in the Saltwater Band and produced his solo albums. He appears in almost every part of the film and often answers questions on Gurrumul's behalf.

questions.stem: Mark Grose appears in the film as:
options: a doctor in Darwin who cared for Gurrumul during his long illness
a teacher at the school Gurrumul attended as a child on Elcho Island
a television host who interviewed Gurrumul in Sydney before his first big national concert
a co-founder of Skinnyfish Music, the Darwin label behind Gurrumul's records
questions.explanation: Grose and Hohnen ran Skinnyfish Music, which works with Indigenous musicians. Like Hohnen, Grose is shown dealing with the fallout when Gurrumul misses the American tour.

questions.stem: In one scene, Hohnen shaves Gurrumul with a cut-throat razor. What does the scene suggest?
options: That Gurrumul is too ill to look after himself
The deep trust and closeness between the two men
That Gurrumul sees Hohnen mainly as his business manager
That Gurrumul is preparing for a tour overseas
questions.explanation: Letting someone shave you with a razor takes great trust. The director chose to show the friendship tenderly, and this quiet moment says more than an interview could.

questions.stem: Gurrumul was blind from birth. How did he play the guitar?
options: Left-handed, on a left-handed guitar built specially for him
Left-handed, on a right-handed guitar held upside down
Right-handed, on a guitar restrung for a left-handed player
With the guitar flat on his lap, played like a keyboard
questions.explanation: Gurrumul taught himself several instruments as a child. Playing a right-handed guitar upside down is one of the details that shows how individual his musicianship was.

questions.stem: What do members of Gurrumul's family contribute to the film?
options: Performances of their own songs, which replace Gurrumul's music in the final scenes
Little, as the film relies on Hohnen and Grose to explain his life and his music
Memories of his childhood, and explanations of the songs and culture behind his music
Criticism of Hohnen and Grose for taking Gurrumul away from his community for good
questions.explanation: Family members talk about Gurrumul as a boy and about the songlines his singing draws on. Their voices place his music inside Yolngu culture, not just the music industry.

questions.stem: Gurrumul rarely speaks in interviews in the film. What context helps explain this, beyond shyness?
options: Under Yolngu custom his role was to sing, while elders spoke publicly
His manager advised him to keep an air of mystery for publicity
He was contractually bound to leave interviews to his record label's staff
Yolngu custom forbids men from speaking in front of a camera
questions.explanation: Gurrumul was shy, but there was also a cultural reason: his role was to sing, and senior people spoke for the community. Reading his silence only as a personality trait misses this.

questions.stem: How does the film present Hohnen's role in Gurrumul's career?
options: Hostile, as he argues with Gurrumul's family throughout the film about money
Devoted and loving, but also caught between Gurrumul's priorities and an industry's demands
Selfish and controlling, using Gurrumul's talent to make himself rich and famous
Distant and businesslike, leaving the care of Gurrumul mostly to his family
questions.explanation: Hohnen clearly loves Gurrumul, but he also has to answer to promoters and audiences. The missed American tour shows the strain of that position.

questions.stem: Where was Gurrumul's home?
options: Galiwin'ku, on Elcho Island in north-east Arnhem Land
Alice Springs, in the centre of the Northern Territory
Thursday Island, in the Torres Strait off Queensland
Broome, on the north-west coast of Western Australia
questions.explanation: Gurrumul grew up in Galiwin'ku on Elcho Island and kept living there even after he became famous. The film keeps returning to the island.

questions.stem: Before his solo career, Gurrumul played in which bands?
options: Yothu Yindi and the Saltwater Band
Midnight Oil and Coloured Stone
No Fixed Address and Warumpi Band
The Bushwackers and Tiddas
questions.explanation: Gurrumul played with Yothu Yindi and later co-led the Saltwater Band. His 2008 solo album, Gurrumul, made him famous around the world.

questions.stem: Yolngu custom generally retires the name and image of a person who has died. Why does the film use his name and image?
options: The record label owned the rights, so the family was not asked for permission
The film was made mainly for overseas audiences, who are not bound by the custom
His family gave permission, so that his legacy would be preserved
The film was released before he died, so the custom did not apply to the film
questions.explanation: His family allowed his name and image to be used publicly again, so that his contribution would not be forgotten.

questions.stem: After his death, and before the family's permission, how was he referred to publicly?
options: As the Singer from Elcho
As Mr Hohnen's brother
By his Yothu Yindi name
As Dr G. Yunupingu
questions.explanation: Avoiding a dead person's first name is part of grieving practice in many Aboriginal communities. 'Dr' comes from an honorary doctorate he received from the University of Sydney.

questions.stem: Gurrumul performed for Queen Elizabeth II and US President Barack Obama while still living on Elcho Island. What does the film suggest about this mix of two worlds?
options: That it was not always easy for him to balance them
That he left the island for good once he was famous
That his family wanted him to stop performing at home
That he preferred concerts overseas to life at home
questions.explanation: Gurrumul kept his home and obligations on Elcho Island while performing for world leaders. Reviewers noted that the film makes clear this mix was not always easy.

questions.stem: The makers agreed that the film would not deal with Gurrumul's health, and chose to show Yolngu culture with pride rather than despair. Why might they have made these choices?
options: To protect his dignity, and to counter films that show Indigenous life only as suffering
Because his illness was unknown to them and to his family until after the film was made
Because a film about illness could not have been screened at major film festivals
To keep the focus on his music career rather than on his family, culture and Country
questions.explanation: The producers have said an elder asked them to present the community's dignity. Leaving out his illness keeps the focus on his music, family and culture.

questions.stem: Which tension is most central to the film?
options: Between Elcho Island and Darwin, which compete to host the biggest music festival
Between the Yolngu and the government over who owns the rights to his recordings
Between Gurrumul's family, culture and Country and the demands of a global music career
Between Gurrumul and Hohnen, who disagree about which songs to put on each album
questions.explanation: The industry wants tours, interviews and sales; Gurrumul's priorities are family, ceremony and home. The film keeps showing these two worlds pulling against each other.

questions.stem: What does the film suggest about how success should be measured?
options: That a musician's worth is best judged by how many awards he has won
That by Yolngu values, family and culture matter more than fame or sales
That success is measured by the number of countries a musician has toured
That Gurrumul failed because he would not do what the industry asked of him
questions.explanation: Some of Gurrumul's choices look like failures to the music industry, such as the missed tour. The film invites the audience to see them by a different measure.

questions.stem: How does the film present the friendship between Gurrumul and Hohnen?
options: As a close, brotherly bond across two cultures, tested by the pressures of fame
As a business deal in which neither man cares much for the other beyond the money it brings
As a rivalry between two musicians competing for the same audiences
As a friendship that ends badly after an argument about the American tour
questions.explanation: The two men are shown as brothers in all but blood, joking backstage and working closely in the studio. The pressures of the industry strain the friendship but don't break it.

questions.stem: What does the film suggest about the songs Gurrumul sings?
options: Most are covers of English pop songs that he translated as a young man
Most were written by Hohnen and then translated into Yolngu for him to sing
They are mostly new songs that deliberately break away from Yolngu tradition
Many are ancient Yolngu songs, and his music helps keep that culture alive
questions.explanation: The film stresses that some of the songs are many thousands of years old and tied to Country and family. His success carried them to audiences around the world.

questions.stem: At times the film lets the picture fade or go dark while the music continues. What is the effect?
options: It suggests that Gurrumul's memories are fading as his illness grows worse
It puts the audience closer to how Gurrumul, who was blind, experienced the world
It hides footage that Gurrumul's family asked the filmmakers to cut from the final version
It marks a change from one year to the next in Gurrumul's career
questions.explanation: The makers describe the film as led by sound. Removing images makes the audience listen as Gurrumul did, and puts his voice at the centre.

questions.stem: The film includes old home movies of Gurrumul's childhood and youth. Why use this archival footage?
options: It shows how much fame changed him, by contrasting his youth with his later life
It shows audiences what Elcho Island will look like in the future
It shows the community and family that shaped him before he was famous
It proves that Gurrumul had already been famous as a child performer
questions.explanation: Home movies let the audience see Gurrumul and Galiwin'ku long before the concerts and awards, grounding his story in family and place.

questions.stem: Much of the film is observational, following Gurrumul backstage, on tour and in the studio. What does this approach allow?
options: It allows the film to recreate key events from his childhood using actors
It means the film can be made without asking Gurrumul for his permission
It shows his personality and choices directly, since he rarely explains himself
It lets an expert narrator explain the meaning of each scene to the audience
questions.explanation: Gurrumul seldom talks about himself, so the camera watches instead: joking with friends, declining an interview he dislikes, working on songs. Actions speak for him.

questions.stem: Gurrumul and his family speak Yolngu languages in the film. How are their words presented?
options: With an English voiceover by an actor, so the original words are hard to hear
Without translation, so that the sound of the language alone carries the meaning
Through Hohnen, who translates their words into English for the camera
With English subtitles, so their own voices are heard rather than replaced
questions.explanation: The film is in English and Yolngu Matha, with subtitles. Hearing people in their own languages respects them and reminds the audience whose story this is.

questions.stem: In its closing stages, the film plays Gurrumul's orchestral music over images of the people of Elcho Island. What is the effect?
options: It hints that the orchestra has replaced Yolngu song on the island
It closes on a celebration of his music and community, not on his death
It suggests that his music will be forgotten by audiences once the film has come to an end
It shows that Gurrumul has left his community to live in the city
questions.explanation: The producers wanted the ending to be a celebration. Linking his last music to his people suggests his legacy lives on in them.

questions.stem: The Gumatj word 'wawa' describes how Gurrumul and Hohnen were regarded. What does it mean?
options: Brother
Teacher
Singer
Stranger
questions.explanation: Under Gumatj custom the two men were regarded as brothers. The word shows how Hohnen was brought into Gurrumul's kinship world.

questions.stem: His final album is called Djarimirri. What is its English subtitle?
options: Song of the Saltwater
Voice of the Island
Home to Country
Child of the Rainbow
questions.explanation: The album's full title is Djarimirri (Child of the Rainbow). It is the orchestral project the film builds to.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest topic sentence for the prompt 'Gurrumul shows a man who would not let fame change him.' Discuss.
options: Gurrumul was a singer from Elcho Island who was in Yothu Yindi and the Saltwater Band
Williams shows that Gurrumul's loyalty to family and Country outweighed fame's demands
Gurrumul is a documentary directed by Paul Damien Williams that was released in 2018
This essay will discuss fame and how it is shown in the documentary Gurrumul
questions.explanation: A strong topic sentence takes a position on the prompt and names what the paragraph will prove. The others retell, announce or state facts without making an argument.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'Gurrumul didn't go on the American tour.' How could this be turned into analysis?
options: Add the names of the American cities where the concerts were going to be held
Describe what Hohnen was wearing when he phoned the American promoters
List the songs that Gurrumul would have sung if he had gone on the tour
Explain how the missed tour shows his obligations at home outweighing the industry's
questions.explanation: Analysis explains what the evidence suggests. Linking the missed tour to the clash between Yolngu priorities and the music industry turns an event into an argument.
